A.explanation: Power is work divided by time, so a force-extension area with units of $\text{N m} = \text{J}$ cannot be power in $\text{W}$.

B.explanation: Stretching may warm the wire slightly, but temperature change is not the area and is not measured in joules.

C.explanation: The graph has no time axis, so the area under force against extension in $\text{m}$ cannot give a time in $\text{s}$.

D.explanation: Work done is $F \times x$ for small steps, so the sum under the force-extension curve is the work done on the wire, stored partly as elastic potential energy.

hints: Look at the axes of the diagram: vertical force in $\text{N}$ and horizontal extension in $\text{m}$ - multiply their units to see what the area must measure.
Recall that a small amount of work is $\Delta W = F \Delta x$, so adding strips of $F$ times $\Delta x$ along the extension axis builds up the total area.
Check why the curved shape past the straight-line region still counts: the area rule for work applies even when force is not proportional to extension.
walkthrough: Identify the given graph: $y$-axis is force $F$ and $x$-axis is extension $x$, starting at $0$ and rising linearly then curving to a maximum.
State the physical rule: work done by a varying force is the sum of $F \Delta x$ for each small extension, which is the area under an $F$-$x$ graph.
Check units: $\text{N} \times \text{m} = \text{J}$, which is the unit of work and energy, not power, temperature or time.
Note this holds for the whole curve, including the non-linear plastic region shown, because each narrow strip still contributes $F$ times its small $\Delta x$.
Therefore the total area represents the work done on the wire to stretch it. This is option D
